en: In the *Jianze qushi xingxiang* (Gradual Method for Explaining the Characteristics of Practice) composed by the Śramaṇa Zhànrán of Bīlíng during the Táng dynasty, it says: "The gradual is like a ladder and a stone step. Regarding the ladder (*tí*):
the *Shuowen jiezi* states that it is a wooden flight of stairs. For reaching extreme heights, one uses a ladder; for moderate heights, one uses a stone step (*dèng*). Therefore...
The eighth fascicle of the Great Sūtra states:
"In order to transform and deliver all the worlds,
he manifests various distinct appearances."
It is like those stairs.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 40, states:
"For example, it is easy to ascend a tower if one has a ladder."
The eighty-eighth [fascicle] says:
"For example, it is like ascending a ladder; starting from the first rung and gradually moving upward, although the higher point is distant, one is nonetheless able to reach it."
Therefore, it is used as a metaphor for gradual progression.
The character "deng" (磴) may also be written with the radical for "feet" (足), meaning to step upward; that which uses the radical for "wood" (木) [is likewise appropriate].
This is not what is used here.
"From stone" refers to mountain slopes that gradually rise in height.
It may also be used in its semantic sense.
It should properly follow the "阜" (mountain/embankment) radical; this character "隥" is likewise a type of ladder.
It can cause one to ascend;
for it begins with the human and celestial realms and culminates in the ultimate reality (*tathatā*).
As for the "Vajra Jewel":
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, fascicle 22, states:
"Just as when a diamond jewel is placed in the sunlight, its color is indeterminate,
so too is the diamond-like samādhi (*vajrasamādhi*)."
If it is among a great assembly, its color is not fixed.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 38, further states:
"It is like a crystal bead which changes according to the colors before it, having no fixed color of its own."
All phenomena are likewise:
some are permanent, others impermanent.
The sūtra follows this single principle throughout all its various practices.
The treatise applies a single principle to all principles;
although the principles and practices differ, they share the same name of "indeterminate.
Therefore, although the names of the vajra and crystal beads differ, their illustrative meaning is identical.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 59, states:
"The vajra-jewel is that which Śakra wields;
when he fought with the asuras, it shattered and fell into Jambudvīpa."
The commentary states:
Principle and practice are like the pearl;
the teaching is like the sun.
Sentient beings are like all other objects;
the contemplation is like the manifestation of forms.
This is the Perfect and Sudden [teaching].
"Complete" (*yuan*) means perfectly integrated and perfect;
"sudden" (*dun*) means immediate, ultimate, and sufficient.
Furthermore, "complete" signifies totality.
Li Qi said: "Yuan" means a round coin;
that is, it is perfectly round and without defect.
Because its essence is not formed gradually, it is called "sudden.
Although its essence is already fully perfected, one must employ twenty-five dharmas as preliminary expedients (*pūrvaprayoga*),
and ten dharmas for the accomplishment of contemplation as the actual cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
The brief explanations in the present preface are fully detailed as follows in the main text.
Regarding those who "pass through" or "soar into the air":
because the space near the earth and the space at ten-thousand-fathom heights share the same substance, they are said to be non-dual.
"Passing through" is a metaphor for the practitioner of the sudden path;
"leaping up" is a metaphor for cultivating practice and contemplating the principle;
and "emptiness" is a metaphor for the non-duality of the sudden principle.
Regarding the phrase "for the three faculties" and so forth:
these three forms of śamatha and vipaśyanā differ according to the faculties;
although their specific manifestations vary, they equally take the sudden principle as their object.
Apart from the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), there are no separate root-natures (genxing).
One should know that these three are all based on the principle of perfection (yuanli) and are distinguished as three types of practice, termed the three root-natures.
Therefore, the gradual approach is not different from the distinct [teachings].
Alternatively, it may be attained by practicing for a single day, a single month, or a single lifetime.
Thus, in the tenth fascicle of the *Xuánwén*, within the section on the classification of teachings (*jiàojiāng*), it says:
"As for those who practice gradual contemplation, from the initial generation of the bodhicitta, they are directed toward the ultimate perfection."
By practicing *ānāpānasmṛti* up to the stage of non-action (*anabhisamskāra*),
it is known that for those of sudden capacity, both realization and practice are simultaneous;
whereas for those of gradual capacity, realization is sudden while practice is gradual.
Regarding the indeterminate liberation and sudden or gradual practice,
some say that these are distinct [categories], yet they fail to perceive the intent of the text.
In the subsequent detailed explanation, first there is the summary that concludes the preceding section and introduces the following one.
First, regarding the explanation of the gradual [approach], it says: "The gradual approach also initially knows the reality of the marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth."
This means that one gives rise to sudden understanding based on the principle of suddenness;
it is said "also knows" in relation to those of the sudden type,
and it is said "difficult to understand" because the understanding arises based on the sudden [approach].
To initiate practice based on understanding is called "difficult practice";
to proceed gradually is called "easy practice" because it is easy to understand.
Although the texts mention them alternately, the terminology necessarily encompasses both.
To resolve difficult-to-understand principles, a gradual practice is initiated.
Within this, there are five stages of progression,
yet thirteen meanings.
Regarding the five stages: first, taking refuge and receiving the precepts;
second, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Third, the three untainted states;
fourth, compassion and loving-kindness;
fifth, the true mark.
Regarding the thirteen meanings,
the first section contains six items,
namely: the three unwholesome [paths of action] and the three wholesome [paths of action].
The third set of four refers to the two vehicles of the two teachings;
together with the previous six meanings, these constitute ten.
The remaining three are not further divided, thus making thirteen in total.
Among these thirteen, the true nature (*dharmatā*) is the object of focus (*ālambana*).
Since it is identical from the perspective of sudden realization, it should not be counted as a distinct limit.
Therefore, in the subsequent question-and-answer section, it says:
There are twelve differences within the gradual [process];
this is precisely what is meant here.
These points are briefly indicated now so that they will be easy to understand later on.
Regarding "the indefinite followed by the sudden":
because the gradual [teachings] are listed in sequence before the indefinite, they are called the "prior gradual";
because the perfect and sudden [teaching] is listed after the text on the indefinite, it is called the "subsequent sudden."
In the second version, the section on the "Indeterminate" is placed after the "Gradual" and "Sudden.
It states that the term "indeterminate" refers to the preceding gradual and sudden approaches;
because it may be either gradual or sudden rather than being restricted to a single method, it is called "indeterminate."
If one proceeds from the beginning to the end, treating the gradual as sudden, only then can it be called "gradual-sudden.
One should know that this is not fixed, for at the outset one may also realize the perfect.
To further explain the characteristics of the non-fixed, one must proceed both forward and backward.
The preceding and succeeding [stages] are simply the gradual and the sudden, respectively.
At times one contemplates the sudden, and at times one contemplates the gradual.
As for "shallow and deep":
Regarding the mutual discussion of the shallow and the deep across the first five sections,
as for phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*li*): sometimes that which is within the realm is taken as phenomenon, and that which is outside the realm is taken as principle.
The ultimate truth and the conventional truth, as well as the three [levels of] *siddhi* and the one *siddhi*, are likewise mutually related.
Here, although many dharmas are presented, when discussing their modes of activity (*ākāra*), they do not transcend these two: the four *siddhis* and *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
As with the aforementioned "settling the mind" (*anxin*) and "pervasive destruction" (*po bian*),
these also do not transcend this [framework], and are therefore listed here.
From the word "or" (*huo*) onwards, the nature of the indeterminate (*aniyata*) is explained.
The text contains two pairs of categories.
The first is based on the four *siddhāntas*.
Regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), they correspond to the world-siddhānta (*loka-siddhānta*), as seen in the initial contemplation of the aggregates and sense bases (*āyatana*).
One then contemplates the aggregates (skandhas) and sense bases (āyatanas) as the primary meaning (paramārtha).
To designate the mundane world as the primary meaning is like contemplating ultimate truth;
it can only give rise to the wholesome and extinguish the unwholesome.
Designating the ultimate truth as the first and the conventional as the second constitutes the two truths.
Next, regarding the application of śamatha and vipaśyanā:
either one may correctly employ vipaśyanā, or it may be appropriate to suspend vipaśyanā.
Alternatively, while correctly employing stillness (*śamatha*), one should employ illumination (*vipaśyanā*) within that stillness.
Because illumination is employed within stillness, stillness itself becomes insight (*vipaśyanā*);
because insight is employed within stillness, insight itself becomes stillness (*śamatha*).
Alternatively, although there may be no dullness or distraction, if one's progress on the path is slight,
such that afflictions are not destroyed and ultimate truth is not revealed,
one must in all cases change one's course through either cessation or illumination.
Therefore, observing that which is accomplished and resting in that which is accomplished, as well as illuminating that which is accomplished—
because these differ from the standard ritual procedures,
they are called "unfixed. In the subsequent section on analysis, within the discussion of the unfixed, four instances refer to these two pairs.
The doubter says, "Let us proceed.
Examining the preceding text,
regarding the phrase "the objects of the teachings and so forth" mentioned in the initial inquiry:
Since they are equally Mahāyāna teachings, equally take the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) as their object, and are equally termed "calm abiding and insight" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*),
why is it that these three types of practice differ so abruptly in their modes of activity?
Next, the answer follows from below.
First is the general response.
Regarding the phrase "whether identical or not identical," etc.:
What prevents three [factors] from being identical when their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are distinct?
Although they are said to be identical in being three, what prevents their modes of activity from being distinct?
This is answered within the gradual progression of the distinctions.
One should name them "gradual" (*ānupūrvika*) and "indeterminate" (*aniyata*) in contrast to the "sudden and perfect" (*yuganaddha*) to distinguish their similarities and differences.
In the present text, however, it merely explains the characteristics of the gradual practice and concludes later by stating, "therefore it is called indeterminate."
Because the indeterminate dharmas (aniyata-dharma) have no fixed stages,
they are appended at the end of the gradual [stages] to conclude the section on the indeterminate.
Within these gradual stages, there are twelve distinct variations, as analyzed previously.
The two teachings and the two vehicles constitute four types of those without outflows (anāsrava).
Why, then, does it now state that among the general category of those without outflows there are three?
To distinguish them individually, they are divided into four types of persons.
If one were to designate them collectively as "untainted" (anāsrava), the three individuals would be subsumed and only a single status would remain.
Now, by citing the collective and subsuming it within the opening of the one, all three are included.
Therefore, it is called the third among the three general categories of the untainted (*anāsrava*).
If one omits the original category and divides them separately, there are four:
namely, the three each for the wholesome and the unwholesome, together with one each for meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and compassion (*karuṇā*).
Thus, they constitute twelve.
If one follows the untainted [dharmas] by dividing them into four distinct categories,
then compassion and loving-kindness should likewise each have three different types.
The absence of [specific] textual descriptions is an abbreviation.
As for the statement that they follow the majority, it is called "gradual and indeterminate" because their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are not fixed in sequence and are manifold;
however, from the perspective of ultimate principle (*tattva*), they are neither many nor few.
In terms of their characteristics, the Sudden [teaching] has two less and the Gradual has two more.
Within the Gradual, the Real Aspect and the Perfect-Sudden share the same characteristics; they need not be explained separately.
Therefore, he merely establishes two points of difference from the Perfect [Teaching] to explain the aforementioned similarities and differences.
Next, regarding the question asked again after the passage "from this chapter onward, it accords with the Mahāyāna":
Although it was previously clarified that the gradual and the indeterminate are not the same,
he again asked three times about their distinctions; therefore,
he once more poses the same question regarding the three distinctions.
Therefore, the objection is formulated: "How can this be called 'discriminating the differences'?
Furthermore, the initial questioner, while admitting that there are three distinct differences, proceeds to ask about their identity.
Therefore, the concluding text states: "The characteristics are suddenly and thus different.
The intention of the subsequent question is that, because the previous answer was different, one asks about the same point using a different phrasing.
Therefore, the commentary concludes by asking: "Why is it called 'Discriminating' (Vibhaṅga)?
Although these two questions are presented together and both precede the third, the intended meaning of the text actually employs the two meanings alternately.
Therefore, both answers state that they are "the same" or "not the same," and so forth.
Furthermore, because the previous answer only presented the characteristics of the gradual (*krama*) as a contrast to the sudden (*akrama*),
the characteristics of the indeterminate (*aniyata*) are clarified by means of the gradual.
Now, wishing to fully distinguish the differences between the three types of characteristics,
[the author] again raises the inquiry by means of the three commonalities;
thus, in the response below, both characteristics are set forth in full.

Regarding this chapter: since its former title here was "The Chapter Distinguishing Differences" (*Biancha Zhang*), and it is now called "The Three Samenesses," why does this chapter distinguish the differences between the three?
Even if the original title has been discarded, what harm is there in such a question?
However, the subsequent detailed response is similar in meaning to what preceded it.
As for the nine points of difference: among the previous twelve, the three types of support for the untainted (anāsrava) are combined into one.
Thus, there are nine [gradual types] alone;
when these are combined with the four indeterminate types, there are thirteen.
When these gradual and indeterminate types are contrasted with the sudden, three distinct categories are formed.
In principle, the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) that serves as the object of focus in the gradual and indeterminate [approaches] is identical to the principle of the sudden [approach].
However, because two different names were used to answer the questions posed,
it is said that [the classification] follows the majority.
Next, all that follows establishes both identity and difference.
By means of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), it is established that they are different yet identical;
whereas by means of conditioned phenomena, it is established that they are identical yet different.
This is truly because the various sages realize the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas;
since they are able to differentiate by means of this unconditioned, it is called "differentiation.
For instance, when the various Arhats attain the minor unconditioned, they still differentiate the minor.
Therefore, all bodhisattvas attain the great unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and are able to discern the great.
Because this discernment functions through the unconditioned, it is said that they "use the unconditioned dharma.
This is the answer according to the second manuscript.
Within the gradual [process], there are twelve differences;
within the indeterminate, there are four differences.
In total, there are thirteen differences.
If there were no third repetition of the original text,
by what means could the second original text be understood?
Furthermore, since twelve and four would amount to sixteen, how could one speak of thirteen?
The master Biao follows the division from the perspective of analysis and the integration from the perspective of synthesis.

One should understand that the twelve [factors] are based on the analysis of the untainted (*anāsrava*), while the thirteen are based on the integration of the untainted, explained in contrast to the indeterminate.
Question:
Question: Why are the four [immeasurables] opened for those without outflows (*anāsrava*), while compassion (*karuṇā*) is not?
Answer: Even if it were opened, it would not contradict [the principle].
In the *Xuánjiàn guān* (Gradual Contemplation of the Profound), four types of compassion are enumerated;
their expansion or contraction varies according to the context and cannot be standardized. Some say:
Within the general category of the untainted (*anāsrava*), these three are precisely the three contemplations:
the untainted is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and the general is the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
Excellent, excellent!
I have been among the assembly of listeners for over a decade,
yet I have truly never heard such an extraordinary interpretation as this.
The "Middle" is precisely the true reality (bhūtatathatā), and true reality is uniform.
How could it be limited by numerical differences?
This is the first impossibility.
First, regarding the claim that the text of this religious school does not state that "provisional" (jia) serves as the general category,
this is untenable. Among the nine stages of gradual progression, there already exists the untainted (anāsrava).
Compassion (maitrī-karuṇā) and "provisional" (prajñapti) share the same meaning;
they should not be counted twice to make nine by adding three. This is untenable.
If one were to take the three bases of good and evil and multiply them by six, they should only result in nine;
yet now you say there are twelve.
This fourth point is untenable.
Even if one were to combine them with the true aspect (dharmatā), they would only total ten;
yet now you speak of twelve.
This fifth point is untenable.
Furthermore, the second text lacks the phrase "the general [category] of the untainted" and also speaks of "twelve.
Now, these three are correlated with the three contemplations,
while also encompassing the gradual sequence.
It is likewise only twelve;
six are not permissible.
Some say that the various *pratyāhāras* (withdrawals) are themselves the contemplations (*vipaśyanā*).
If cessation is itself the one who ceases,
why is there only cessation and no contemplation in the three miserable realms?
And why is there only contemplation and no cessation in the state of eternal abiding?

If one were to take these as the [four] applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), then there would be four applications of tranquility (śamatha) and four applications of insight (vipaśyanā) in the middle four rounds,
and one application of tranquility and one application of insight in the first and last two rounds;
thus, there would be only ten.
If one were to establish cessation and contemplation separately for both the wholesome and the unwholesome,
there would then be nine distinct types, resulting in eighteen modes of cessation and contemplation.
Furthermore, if one were to enumerate their constant abiding, it would again result in the manifest textual categories.
The text states that there are nine gradual stages.
The seventh [stage] is untenable.
Furthermore, one should reflect that although one may have known the perfection from the very beginning of the gradual process, [it remains so].
They differ only in that during the stages of the Middle Way and the Ten Practices, the duration of the long practice is extensive.
Having briefly understood these two as distinct from the Separate Teaching,
one knows that while these three [teachings] share the same realization of the Perfect Principle, their aspects of practice differ slightly.
One should know that Nanyue transmitted only the principle of the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching] of Tiantai.
Regarding practice, it must be supplemented by the Gradual and Indeterminate [teachings].
Question:
"Does Master Nanyue know the four teachings?
He replied,
"Master Nanyue knows them thoroughly, yet he does not provide detailed classifications."
Why is this? For instance,
the Wise One (Zhizhe) set aside the [standard] stages and cited the usage of Nan Yue, taking the forty-two characters from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* to constitute the Perfect Stages.
The stages such as "Joyful" (pramuditā) are taken as distinct positions (*viśeṣa-bhūmi*),
while the stages such as "Dry Wisdom" (śuklavipaśyanā) are taken as common positions (*sāmānya-bhūmi*).
Furthermore, Nanyue himself explained the forty-two letter-gates (*dvātriṃśadakṣaramukha*).
I have also submitted a commentary on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Dapin jing),
interpreting it according to the threefold teaching.
Since one now understands that throughout the text of the threefold teaching’s *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, the term "vaipulya" (衍) is used in contrast to "pitaka" (藏) to designate the "Lesser" [Vehicle].
Thus we know that Nanyue also understood the four teachings;
furthermore, these four teachings did not originate with Nanyue.
Since Master Huiwen relied upon the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, [he already knew them].
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains the sūtras, and those sūtras clarify the three teachings.
One should know that these teachings have been transmitted for a long time, but their systematic classification flourished only upon reaching Tiantai. Some say:
The testimony of the divine monk regarding the bestowal of these words lacks corroboration;
the divine monk merely said: "From this day forward, whether you act for yourself or transform others, I shall always be your shadow and echo."
Since his innate capacity for samādhi has already blossomed with brilliance,
what need is there for the Four Teachings or divine monks?
His succession to this position is well-founded and deeply accords with the holy intent.
Therefore, the three contemplations (sanzhiguan) comprehensively encompass the four teachings.

Furthermore, although the names of these three types of cessation-and-contemplation (zhiguan) appear similar to the three [teachings] within the eightfold classification of teachings, their characteristics are fundamentally distinct.
Among those eight teachings, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra is designated as the "Sudden" (dun).
Departing for the Deer Park represents the gradual [approach].
It is not fixedly situated within the first four flavors;
in the subsequent section on distinctions, it merely borrows the name.
To raise an objection based on the contrast between the Secret [Teaching] and the Three [Vehicles] is not the correct intention.
Let us set aside the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching].
In the explanation of the Perfect and Sudden [Teaching],
first regarding *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*:
from "initially taking the true reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) as the object" up to "the ultimate truth."
This is precisely the object of focus for śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Although "focusing upon" (ālambana) and "cultivating" (abhisamskāra) belong to the subject who contemplates,
my intention here is primarily to clarify the wondrous object that is focused upon.
Following the explanation of the object of focus, the next section explains the observing subject: namely, mindfulness (*smṛti*) as the binding.
Being tranquil yet constantly illuminating—this is the binding as mindfulness.
It illuminates while remaining eternally quiescent;
since subject and object are already one, how much more so are cessation and contemplation?
Not a single form or a single fragrance is not the Middle Way.
The Middle Way is the Dharma-realm;
the Dharma-realm is cessation and contemplation.
In cessation and contemplation, subject and object are non-dual, merging into one in profound stillness.
Although the objects of focus and mental attention belong to the objective realm,
for the time being, we shall clarify the illuminating and quiescent reflection by means of the subject that cognizes them.
Within the Madhyamaka teachings elucidated by our own mountain school, the Middle Way possesses only two meanings.
First, the avoidance of the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism pertains to the first two teachings;
second, buddha-nature pertains to the latter two teachings.
Within the teaching on buddha-nature, there is both identity and distinction because the teachings are divided into provisional and ultimate.
Now, because we follow the sense of "immediacy," it is said that form and fragrance are none other than the Middle Way.
Although worldly people universally regard such things as form and fragrance to be insentient,
they nonetheless commonly concede that form and fragrance are the Middle Way.
The doctrine of insentient beings possessing Buddha-nature confuses the ears and startles the mind.
For now, let us evaluate it through ten points so that one will not be deluded regarding the principle;
the rest may be understood by analogy. First, with respect to the body.
That which is called Buddha-nature should be complete with the three bodies (trikāya).
One cannot claim that it possesses only the nature of the response body (nirmāṇakāya).
If it possesses the three bodies, and since the dharma body (dharmakāya) is admitted to be all-pervasive, why would it exclude insentient things?
Second, regarding their essence, the three bodies are mutually identical and never separated for even a moment.
Since it is admitted that the *dharmakāya* pervades all places,
the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* have never been apart from the *dharmakāya*.
Moreover, since the Dharma-body is always present within the other two bodies, we know that the three bodies pervade all phenomena; how could it be that only the Dharma-body does so?
If even the Dharma-body alone is pervasive, it still possesses the three bodies—how much more so when they are considered together? How could it be that only the Dharma-body is pervasive?
Third, regarding the distinction between phenomena and principle:
from the perspective of phenomena, there is a division between the sentient and the insentient;
from the perspective of principle, there is no distinction between the insentient and the non-sentient.
Therefore, that which possesses sentience is thus, and that which lacks sentience is likewise so.
Fourth, regarding the lands:
from the perspective of deluded sentiment, the environment and its inhabitants are distinguished.
From the perspective of principle and wisdom, the basis is itself the correct [reality].
Just as the eternally quiescent light is the land of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*),
when body and land are in accord, what separation could there be from the insentient?
Fifth, regarding the distinction between the path of teaching and the path of realization: on the path of teaching, one speaks of sentient beings and non-sentient things;
however, on the path of realization, because they are not dualistic, one cannot distinguish between the two.
Sixth, regarding the ultimate and the conventional:
because it is ultimate, its essence is one; because it is conventional, it is divided into existence and non-existence.
These two are non-dual—this can be understood through reflection.
Seventh, regarding inclusion and subordination:
all phenomena are subordinated to the mind.
Since there is nothing else apart from the mind, how could there be any further distinction or separation?
It merely states that the essence of the sentient being's mind is all-pervasive;
how could it exclude grasses and trees, singling them out as "insentient"?
Eighth is cause and effect.
From the perspective of causes and deluded attachments, they appear distinct and separated;
from the perspective of results and awakening, the Buddha-nature is eternally identical.
Ninth is "according to what is appropriate."
The fourfold analysis follows the *siddhānta*.
While the benefits of the teachings differ, they are here divided into two categories.
Tenth is "in accordance with the teaching."
The Three Teachings state that while there is no teaching of the Perfect [Vehicle], it is universally present.
Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"Because sentient beings are suchness, all dharmas are suchness."

If it were as you suggest— that there is no Buddha-nature according to the principle of the provisional teachings— then the provisional nature of the teaching and the reality of the principle would not accord with our present intent.
Furthermore, if we discuss insentient things, why limit them to external forms alone?
The internal form is likewise so.
Therefore, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* says:
"This body is insentient, like grass, wood, tiles, or pebbles."
If we discuss sentient beings, it is not only living creatures; everything is solely mind.
Thus, a single speck of dust is fully endowed with the Buddha-nature of all sentient beings, and is likewise endowed with the Buddha-nature of all Buddhas of the ten directions.
From the perspective of departing from one's own realm, the truths are clarified as being sudden;
this refers specifically to the truth of non-action (anabhisaṃskāra).
Within the Four Great Vows, the characteristics of the truths are explained in brief.
This briefly demonstrates the contemplation of non-action (*anabhisamskāra*).
Therefore, the commentary on the four foundations of mindfulness explains the four noble truths of non-action as follows:
"The suffering of the ten realms contained within a single thought-moment is called the truth of suffering."
The afflictions of the ten realms are called the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya).
Suffering itself as nirvana is called the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya).
Afflictions themselves as awakening are called the Truth of the Path (mārga-satya).
Next, departing from the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), one uses only cessation and contemplation (śamatha-vipaśyanā) to conclude the unconditioned truth (anabhisaṃskāra-satya).
Next, one concludes that the essence is non-dual.
Departing from the gradual and the indeterminate, one extensively cites evidence to establish the perfection [of the teaching].
First, we shall briefly examine two points;
next, we will formally cite scriptural evidence.
Since we have already provided both detailed and concise explanations, and now again cite evidence, it is said that this further clarifies the matter.

Possessing both afflictions and delusions is likened to being stung by mosquitoes and gadflies;

Regarding the term "wondrous retribution":

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who have not heard of the wondrous rewards and merits of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*);
because their efforts would otherwise be in vain, the wondrous rewards are taught to comfort and gladden them.
What is meant by "tearing the great net" up to "escaping the cage"?
"Breaking" means to tear asunder.

Although one has already experienced the fruition of [past] karma and established teachings to benefit others by breaking through the nets of doubt in others, though this was originally intended to open the eye of wisdom for sentient beings, their karmic capacity has not yet manifested.

Just as prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, sentient beings were mutually confused regarding the provisional and the real, emptiness and existence, and phenomena and principle within the teachings;
if one is to make a definitive judgment, one must open up the provisional and manifest the real so that the provisional and the real do not become conflated.
This enables one to understand the fundamental intent of the teachings,
to shatter the web of doubts regarding those teachings, and to penetrate the single principle that nothing exists outside it.
It allows for the realization of the great essence of the Dharma-gates and the knowledge that all various teachings have a point of convergence.
Regarding the phrase "hearing of snow is called cold" and so forth,
this cites scriptural evidence for those who cling to the literal teaching while being deluded regarding its essential meaning.
Thus, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 13, states:
Within the Buddha-dharma, they have surreptitiously appropriated a small portion and falsely conceptualized it as possessing permanence, bliss, self, and purity,
like a person born blind who cannot recognize the color of milk.
He then asked him,
"What does milk resemble?
The other replied:
The color of the milk was white like a conch shell.
The blind man asked again,
"Is the color of this milk like the sound of a conch shell?"
He replied, "No. He asked again,
"What is it like?"
He replied,
"It is like rice powder.
The blind man spoke again.
"Is it as soft as the color of rice powder? He replied, "No."
The blind man spoke again:
"What does rice flour resemble?
He replied:
"It is like snow.
The blind man asked again,
"Is snow cold?"
He replied,
"No. The blind man asked again.
To what is it similar?
He replied:
"It is like a crane."
The blind man spoke again,
"Is it like the movement of a crane?
He replied:
"No. Although the blind man hears these four descriptions,
he can never see the true color of the milk."
The same applies to the non-Buddhists:
although they hear the four names, they ultimately cannot understand the intended meaning of the terms "permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
They are like those blind people who are confused about the true color of milk.
Those who are currently confused about the teachings can be understood by analogy with this.
As for the present discussion on "harmonization" and so forth:
in principle, there is fundamentally no teaching; any teaching must necessarily accord with the capacities of sentient beings.
The four *siddhāntas*, the four gates, the various contemplations, and the various truths were suited to the times and benefited beings, yet they had not reached universal application;
consequently, each adhered to a single corner [of the truth], and their emotional attachments remained unbroken.
Now, for the sake of harmonizing these, former doubts suddenly vanish.
It is like a caged bird whose spirit finds no comfort;
by releasing its stubborn attachments and opening the cage of provisional teachings,
it is as if wandering through the great void, unimpeded in its vast extent.
If those who are blind from birth, even though they do not recognize milk,
do not yet grasp at shells and the like to give rise to disputes,
how much more so for those who have returned to the Great Abode and reached the Sovereign?
Having completed the transformation of sentient beings, one returns to the secret treasury (*guhyakośa*).
The essence of this secret treasury is without beginning or end;
though without beginning, it initiates itself.
One first cultivates the three contemplations;
though they have no end, they culminate in the ultimate end which reaches the three virtues.
Though they have no obstruction, they are provisionally named the three hindrances.
Though there is no actual supernatural penetration (*abhijñā*), it is conventionally designated as the three virtues (*guṇa*).
The initial passage concerns the dharma of principle (*li-fa*);
from "if one knows" onwards concerns that which is attained through cultivation (*xiu-de*).
If one attains this intent, why would there be anything other than mastery and unimpededness upon reaching the fruit?
Even during the stage of the cause, one realizes that the beginning and the end are non-dual.
